title: A Physics Informed Bayesian Neural Network for the Neutron Star Equation of State
summary: We present a physics-informed Bayesian neural-network framework to infer neutron-star equations of state from theoretical priors and to propagate the associated uncertainties to stellar observables. Trained on a large and representative ensemble of hadronic EoSs, the model learns $P(ε)$ via stochastic variational inference, incorporating soft constraints at saturation density and from perturbative QCD, together with penalties enforcing monotonicity and causality. The accepted core EoSs are matched to an SLy4 crust and evolved through a unified Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff-plus-tidal solver to generate posterior predictions in the mass-radius ($M$-$R$) and mass-tidal-deformability ($M$-$Λ$) planes. The inferred posterior is consistent with NICER radius measurements and the observed $2.0\,M_\odot$ maximum-mass constraint, yielding $R_{1.4}=12.1^{+1.4}_{-0.9}\,\mathrm{km}$, $Λ_{1.4}=580^{+520}_{-240}$, and $M_{\mathrm{max}}\simeq 2.11\pm0.05\,M_\odot$ (90\% CI). The resulting canonical tidal deformability can be assessed \emph{a posteriori} against current gravitational-wave constraints. Overall, this framework provides a flexible, non-parametric mapping from microphysical EoS uncertainties to neutron-star observables.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian neural-network framework infers neutron-star equations of state from theoretical models and physical constraints, producing uncertainty-propagated, observationally consistent predictions of neutron-star properties.
AI.motivation: To robustly infer neutron-star EoS and related uncertainties affecting observations.
AI.method: A physics-informed Bayesian neural-network trained on a large ensemble of hadronic EoSs using stochastic variational inference, incorporating physical constraints like monotonicity, causality, saturation density, and perturbative QCD, with subsequent integration via a Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff-plus-tidal solver for observable predictions.
AI.result: The model produces posterior predictions for neutron-star mass-radius and mass-tidal-deformability relationships consistent with observational data (NICER radius measurements and maximum mass constraints), yielding credible intervals for radius, tidal deformability, and maximum mass of neutron stars.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a flexible, non-parametric approach to map uncertainties in microphysical EoS to neutron-star observables, enabling post-hoc assessment of tidal deformability against gravitational-wave data.

title: Pair-Rich Corona of an Accreting Kerr Black Hole
comment: 30 pages, 23 figures, submitted to the Astrophysical Journal
summary: We build a self-consistent model of a warm scattering corona near an accreting black hole in Kerr geometry, in the regime of slow ($\sim 0.01$ Eddington) mass accretion. An iterative Monte Carlo procedure is developed that incorporates self-consistently the effects of Compton scattering and electron-positron pair creation, as well as general relativistic lensing and frame dragging effects. Soft thermal photons are seeded in the inner disk and the velocity dispersion of the electrons and positrons adjusted to yield a fixed seed luminosity amplification through Compton scattering. A simple kinematic prescription is also added for bulk outflow. Pair creation by photon collisions raises significantly the density of scattering charges in and around the innermost ion disk, which is assumed to be geometrically thick and rarefied compared with the disk outside 10 gravitational radii. The self-consistent pair cloud is concentrated closer to the BH. The spectrum and polarization of the escaping X-rays are recorded as a function of the observer's orientation. The temperature and Compton parameter measured from the output spectra using the compPS package are consistent with fits to binary BH data in the hardest spectral state; the polarization degree rises to $4-10\%$ through the 2-8 keV band with allowance for $e^\pm$ upflow from the BH equator.

AI.tldr: A self-consistent Monte Carlo model of a warm scattering corona near a slowly accreting Kerr black hole successfully explains observed X-ray spectra and polarization by including pair creation and relativistic effects.
AI.motivation: To create a self-consistent model of the corona near an accreting black hole that accounts for physical processes affecting X-ray spectrum and polarization, particularly in the slow accretion regime (~0.01 Eddington).
AI.method: An iterative Monte Carlo procedure incorporating Compton scattering, electron-positron pair creation, general relativistic lensing, and frame dragging is developed to model the warm scattering corona near an accreting Kerr black hole at low accretion rates.
AI.result: The model shows significant pair creation enhancing scattering charge density near the black hole, producing X-ray spectra and polarization consistent with binary black hole observations in the hardest spectral state, with polarization degrees rising to 4-10% in the 2-8 keV band.
AI.conclusion: The inclusion of pair creation and relativistic effects in the corona model yields predicted spectra and polarization in good agreement with observations, supporting the model's validity for accreting black holes in the low accretion regime.

title: Moving-Mesh Simulations of Mini-Common Envelope Ejection in Classical Novae
summary: Although well studied, our understanding of the mass ejection mechanisms of cataclysmic variables remains incomplete. Recent work suggests that binary interaction plays an important role in driving and shaping this mass ejection and may affect the long-term evolution of the system. In this paper, we perform a three-dimensional moving-mesh hydrodynamic simulation of a cataclysmic variable system to study the effect of binary interaction on mass ejection. We find that once the flow crosses the ${\rm L}_1$ Lagrange point, the material is ejected roughly isotropically. This can be seen in a roughly spherical distribution of the ejecta at large radii. We also show that the ${\rm L}_2$ Lagrange point is not important in the ejection of mass, contrary to the assumption in some previous work in this area. Finally, we find that the specific angular momentum of the ejected material is larger than its initial specific angular momentum. This enhanced angular momentum ejection likely affects the long-term evolution of the binary system.

AI.tldr: Using 3D hydrodynamic simulation, the study reveals isotropic mass ejection from the L1 point and enhanced angular momentum in ejecta, impacting the long-term binary evolution.
AI.motivation: To better understand the mass ejection mechanisms influenced by binary interactions in cataclysmic variables, which remain not fully understood and may impact the system's long-term evolution.
AI.method: Three-dimensional moving-mesh hydrodynamic simulation of a cataclysmic variable system.
AI.result: Material crossing the L1 Lagrange point is ejected nearly isotropically with a roughly spherical ejecta distribution; the L2 point does not significantly contribute to mass ejection; ejected material has higher specific angular momentum than initially.
AI.conclusion: Binary interaction drives isotropic mass ejection mainly through the L1 point, not L2, and the increased angular momentum of ejecta likely influences the system's long-term evolution.

title: JWST Constraints on Primordial Magnetic Fields
summary: Primordial magnetic fields (PMFs) enhance small-scale structure formation through the Lorentz force acting on baryons, boosting the abundance of low-mass halos and their hosted galaxies. We show that the reionisation history calibrated with the UV luminosity function (UVLF) provides stringent bounds: strong PMFs induce a characteristic double reionisation at $z \approx 24$ that is incompatible with CMB measurements of the optical depth, yielding $\sqrt{\left\langle B^2 \right\rangle} < 0.27\,{\rm nG}$ and $< 0.18\,{\rm nG}$ for $n_B = -2$ and $n_B = 2$ respectively at $95\%\,{\rm CL}$ using Planck priors on $τ$. This establishes early galaxy observables as among the most sensitive probes of PMFs in Gaussian, non-helical scenarios.

AI.tldr: Primordial magnetic fields boost early structure formation, causing reionisation features incompatible with CMB data, allowing tight constraints on PMF strength using galaxy UV luminosity functions and Planck measurements.
AI.motivation: Constraining primordial magnetic fields via their effect on early galaxy formation and reionisation to improve understanding of early universe conditions.
AI.method: Analyze the impact of PMFs on small-scale structure formation via the Lorentz force on baryons, quantify the resulting enhancement in low-mass halo and galaxy formation, model the reionisation history calibrated with UV luminosity functions, and compare predicted optical depths with Planck CMB measurements to set bounds on PMF strength.
AI.result: Strong PMFs cause a distinctive double reionisation at high redshift (~24), which contradicts current CMB optical depth observations. Using this discrepancy, the study constrains the root-mean-square PMF strength to below 0.27 nG for spectral index nB = -2 and below 0.18 nG for nB = 2 at 95% confidence level.
AI.conclusion: Early galaxy observations and reionisation history provide stringent and sensitive constraints on primordial magnetic fields in Gaussian, non-helical scenarios, tightening the limits on PMF strength beyond previous bounds.

title: Core Collapse Supernova Modeling: The Next Ten Years
comment: Submitted to Classical and Quantum Gravity as part of a Focus Issue on Core Collapse Supernova Gravitational Wave Astronomy and Astrophysics: Past, Present, and Future motivated by the First IGWN Symposium on Core Collapse Supernova Gravitational Wave Theory and Detection held in Warsaw in July 2025
summary: Core collapse supernova modeling has advanced considerably since the first numerical simulations were performed sixty years ago. In particular, the last decade has brought us sophisticated three-dimensional models with significant predictive capabilities -- e.g., for core collapse supernova gravitational wave emission. The six decades of modeling have shown us the importance of individual components of these general relativistic neutrino radiation magnetohydrodynamics events -- specifically, the importance of neutrino kinetics, fluid instabilities, magnetic fields, strong gravity, and the nuclear equation of state and neutrino--matter interactions calculated in a manner consistent with the equation of state. They have also shown us that simulation outcomes are sensitive to variations in the treatment of these ingredients, demanding a level of rigor that has not yet been consistently met by modelers. The efficacy of the neutrino shock reheating mechanism for core collapse supernovae has been demonstrated. The models now require an improved quantitative predictive capability, which will be achieved through increased sophistication in the treatment of model components, both macroscopic (e.g., strong-field gravity) and microscopic (e.g., neutrino--matter interactions). Advancement of core collapse supernova theory will also require the cooperation of modelers in other fields, especially stellar evolution and nuclear theory, to meet the level of rigor required to make the most of the eventuality of a Galactic core collapse supernova and its multimessenger emissions.

AI.tldr: Core collapse supernova modeling has advanced to sophisticated 3D simulations revealing key physical processes and sensitivities; improvement requires enhanced model sophistication and interdisciplinary cooperation.
AI.motivation: To improve the predictive capability of core collapse supernova models by addressing the complex interplay of neutrino kinetics, fluid instabilities, magnetic fields, strong gravity, and the nuclear equation of state with neutrino--matter interactions.
AI.method: Three-dimensional numerical simulations of core collapse supernovae incorporating general relativistic neutrino radiation magnetohydrodynamics.
AI.result: Demonstration of the efficacy of the neutrino shock reheating mechanism and realization that simulation outcomes are sensitive to treatment variations of physical ingredients, necessitating higher rigor in model components.
AI.conclusion: Future progress in core collapse supernova theory depends on more rigorous treatment of model components and collaboration across stellar evolution and nuclear theory to exploit multimessenger observations of Galactic events.

title: spectroxide: A code package for computing cosmic microwave background spectral distortions
summary: We present spectroxide, a code package for computing cosmic microwave background spectral distortions in which all ${\sim}14{,}500$ lines of Rust code, Python interface, and ${\sim}400$ automated tests were written by an AI assistant (Claude Code) under human physicist supervision. The solver evolves the photon Boltzmann equation under Compton scattering, double Compton emission, and Bremsstrahlung from $z \sim 5 \times 10^6$ to the present, computing spectral distortions from arbitrary heat and photon injection within this redshift range. No fully open-source code of this kind is publicly available; we validate against analytic limits, published spectra, and publicly available precomputed Green's function tables. We document the development as a case study in AI-assisted scientific computing, highlighting how domain expertise caught physics bugs (incorrect dimensional prefactors, near-cancellation errors) that evaded the full automated test suite, and provide recommendations for best practices in human--AI collaborative development of scientific software. We make spectroxide publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces 'spectroxide,' an open-source AI-assisted code package that computes cosmic microwave background spectral distortions accurately through numerical evolution of physical processes, validated extensively, showcasing effective human-AI collaboration in scientific software development.
AI.motivation: To develop an open-source, AI-assisted software package capable of accurately computing cosmic microwave background (CMB) spectral distortions, addressing the lack of publicly available tools for this purpose.
AI.method: Developed a code package 'spectroxide' entirely written by an AI assistant (Claude Code) with human physicist supervision; the solver numerically evolves the photon Boltzmann equation, including relevant physical processes (Compton scattering, double Compton emission, Bremsstrahlung) from early universe redshifts ($(z \\sim 5\\times 10^6)$) to the present. Validated results against analytical limits, existing spectra, and precomputed Green's function tables. Documented AI-human collaboration and debugging processes.
AI.result: Produced a fully functional, publicly available open-source codepack 'spectroxide' consisting of ~14,500 Rust code lines, Python interface, and ~400 automated tests that accurately computes CMB spectral distortions. Demonstrated AI-written code quality with human oversight catching subtle physics bugs missed by tests.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted scientific software development is feasible and effective for complex physics computations with proper human domain expertise involvement. This collaboration enhances software quality by catching subtle errors and provides a model for best practices in human-AI co-development in scientific computing.

title: Non-Monotonic Rotation Imprint on Time-Integrated Neutrino Spectral Moments in a 15\,$M_\odot$ Core-Collapse Supernova Sequence
summary: We study the early post-bounce neutrino signal of the published Garching $15\,M_\odot$ rotating core-collapse supernova (CCSN) sequence consisting of non-rotating (NR), slowly rotating (SR, $Ω_0=0.5$ rad\,s$^{-1}$), and fast-rotating (FR, $Ω_0=150$ rad\,s$^{-1}$, artificially boosted ${\sim}300{\times}$) three-dimensional models. We present a new analysis of these publicly available simulation data; no new simulations were performed. Our central result, for this specific model sequence, is that SR and FR shift the integrated spectral moments in \emph{opposite directions} relative to NR: FR drives the spectra toward softer, more-pinched states, while SR moves them weakly toward harder, less-pinched states. Placed in a spectral-shift plane $(Δ\langle E\rangle_L,\,Δα_L)$, NR sits at the origin, and SR and FR occupy \emph{diagonally opposite quadrants}, making the non-monotonic response immediately visible as an anti-correlation in two spectral dimensions simultaneously. The focus is the accretion interval $t_{\rm pb}=0.05$--$0.30$\,s, where the rotation imprint is strongest. Quantitatively, fast rotation produces $Δ\langle E_{ν_e}\rangle_L=-0.513$\,MeV and $Δα_{ν_e}=+0.161$, with corresponding shifts $Δ\langle E_{\barν_e}\rangle_L=-0.440$\,MeV and $Δα_{\barν_e}=+0.173$; the SR shifts are an order of magnitude smaller and in the opposite sense. The fast-rotation signature is coherent across all $15\,488$ lines of sight and is established during early accretion. With only three models from a single progenitor family, this result is a phenomenological characterization of one published sequence and a suggestive indication of a non-monotonic, possibly strongly nonlinear, rotational response within this sequence; the functional form and generality of the dependence on $Ω_0$ remain unconstrained.

AI.tldr: Studying the effect of rotation on neutrino spectra in core-collapse supernova simulations reveals that slow and fast rotation induce opposite spectral shifts during early accretion, indicating a non-monotonic rotational response.
AI.motivation: To understand how different initial rotation rates affect the early post-bounce neutrino emission spectra during the accretion phase of core-collapse supernovae, using spectral moments as diagnostic tools.
AI.method: Analysis of publicly available 3D core-collapse supernova simulation data from Garching for a 15 solar mass progenitor with different initial rotation rates: non-rotating, slowly rotating, and fast rotating models.
AI.result: Slow rotation causes a weak shift in the neutrino spectra toward harder, less-pinched states, while fast rotation shifts the spectra toward softer, more-pinched states, with these shifts being anti-correlated in spectral moment space. Fast rotation produces quantitatively measurable shifts in spectral mean energy and pinching parameters, coherent across all viewing angles. Slow rotation effects are much smaller and opposite in direction.
AI.conclusion: This study phenomenologically characterizes the rotational imprint on neutrino signals in one progenitor family, highlighting a non-monotonic and potentially nonlinear dependence on rotation rate, but further work is needed to understand the generality and functional form of this dependence.

title: Cosmic gas accretion from filaments onto galaxy clusters using the IllustrisTNG simulation
comment: 12 pages, 8 figures, submitted to A&A, comments welcome
summary: Galaxy clusters grow through the matter accretion from the cosmic web, mainly along filaments. We aim to characterize the gas accretion onto clusters, focusing on the role of filaments in driving anisotropic inflows and thermodynamic properties, as it remains a key challenge for cosmology. In this study, we analyzed 415 galaxy clusters from the IllustrisTNG-300 hydrodynamical simulation at $z=0$. Anisotropic signatures are highlighted by probing both isotropically and anisotropically (gas in filaments only), the radial profiles of gas properties (including temperature, entropy, density, and pressure), and the radial velocity distributions. Our results highlight two distinct regimes of gas accretion depending on the cluster-centric distances. In the cluster environment ($\sim$ 2-4$R_{200}$), fast infalling warm gas tunneled by cosmic filaments enters the warm-hot circumcluster medium, but filaments remain colder due to their slow thermalization with the surrounding, generating transverse temperature gradients. At the cluster outskirts ($\sim$ 1-2$R_{200}$), gas infalling along filaments enters the hot intracluster medium, with a strong tangential velocity gradient. Warm gas tends to penetrate clusters from filaments, while hot gas is preferentially ejected beyond them. The mass and dynamical state of clusters significantly impact these accretion features, with relaxed and massive clusters exhibiting stronger and more extended temperature discontinuities. Overall, this work emphasizes a coherent picture of anisotropic gas accretion from filaments onto clusters. While virial shocks tend to be observed near the cluster boundary, especially at the filament-cluster interface. We do not find strong evidence of accretion shocks around filaments, suggesting slow thermalization of filament gas as it enters the dense warm-hot circum-cluster environment.

AI.tldr: This study uses simulations to characterize anisotropic gas accretion onto galaxy clusters through filaments, revealing distinct thermal and velocity structures in different cluster regions and highlighting the lack of strong accretion shocks around filaments.
AI.motivation: The study aims to better understand the role of filaments in the anisotropic gas accretion onto galaxy clusters, addressing a key cosmological challenge by characterizing thermodynamic and kinematic properties of gas inflows that influence cluster growth and evolution.
AI.method: The authors analyze radial profiles of temperature, entropy, density, pressure, and radial velocity distributions of gas in and around 415 galaxy clusters at redshift zero from the IllustrisTNG-300 hydrodynamical simulation, comparing isotropic gas properties to those specifically within filaments to study anisotropic accretion signatures.
AI.result: The paper investigates gas accretion onto galaxy clusters through cosmic filaments using hydrodynamical simulations. It identifies two regimes of anisotropic gas inflow characterized by distinct thermodynamic and kinematic features at different cluster-centric distances. The cluster environment (2-4 R_200) exhibits fast infalling warm gas along filaments with transverse temperature gradients, whereas at the outskirts (1-2 R_200), gas enters the hot intracluster medium showing strong tangential velocity gradients. Filamentary inflows tend to bring warm gas into clusters, while hot gas is generally ejected along filament directions. Cluster mass and dynamical state influence these anisotropic accretion signatures. The study finds virial shocks near cluster boundaries but no strong accretion shocks around filaments, implying slow thermalization of filament gas.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that gas accretion onto clusters via filaments is anisotropic with two distinct radial regimes, influenced by cluster properties. While virial shocks are observed near cluster boundaries, filament gas thermalizes slowly without strong accretion shocks, emphasizing the complex thermodynamic processes governing cluster growth.

title: The GMRT High-Resolution Southern Sky Survey for pulsars and transients -- VIII: Orbital Variability and the Evolution of a 1-Day He-WD Millisecond Pulsar J2101-4208
summary: We present timing and orbital phase-resolved polarimetry of the millisecond pulsar (MSP) J2101$-$4802, having a spin period of 9.48~ms and dispersion measure (DM) $25.05\ \mathrm{pc\ cm^{-3}}$ discovered with the Giant Meter Radio Telescope (GMRT). From the phase-connected timing of this MSP spanning 3.7 years, we identify that PSR J2101-4802 is in a $\sim$1-day binary orbit with a likely helium-white-dwarf (He-WD) companion having a median companion mass of $\simeq0.15\, M_\odot$, consistent with canonical recycling in the Galactic field. The timing solution further reveals an unusually large orbital period derivative, $\dot{P}_b$ ($\sim10^{-11}\,{\rm s\,s}^{-1}$), compared to typical Galactic-field MSP--HeWD binaries, which cannot be explained by the contributions from kinematic effects (Shklovskii and Galactic acceleration) or general-relativistic damping. Using wideband, full-Stokes observations, we also trace the linear and circular polarization variation across the orbital phase and fit a rotating-vector model (RVM) to its position-angle swing across the pulse phase, yielding constraints on the emission geometry (magnetic inclination and impact angle) of this system. The combination of a $\sim$1-day orbit, $\sim0.15\,M_\odot$ companion, modest spin-down power, unusually large $\dot{P}_b$, and phase-locked magnetized intrabinary plasma signatures suggests that PSR~J2101$-$4802 represents a transitional system linking redback-like spiders to detached He--WD MSP binaries.

AI.tldr: This study reports timing and polarization observations of MSP J2101-4802, revealing its 1-day binary orbit with a likely helium white dwarf companion and unusual orbital period derivative, suggesting transitional behavior between redback spiders and detached He-WD MSP binaries.
AI.motivation: To characterize MSP J2101-4802's binary properties, polarization behavior, and orbital dynamics, to understand its evolutionary status and classification within MSP binary categories.
AI.method: The authors performed phase-connected timing over 3.7 years with the GMRT, analyzed binary orbit parameters, measured the orbital period derivative, conducted wideband full-Stokes polarization observations across orbital phases, and applied a rotating-vector model to fit position-angle swings for emission geometry constraints.
AI.result: Discovery of a significant orbital period derivative unexplained by typical kinematic or relativistic effects, identification of emission geometry from polarization analysis, and evidence suggesting the system bridges redback-like spider MSPs and detached He-WD MSP binaries.
AI.conclusion: PSR J2101-4802 is a transitional millisecond pulsar system linking redback spiders and detached helium white dwarf MSP binaries, indicated by its unusual orbital period derivative, companion characteristics, and magnetized intrabinary plasma signatures.

title: Bound or blown: the fate of hot gas in galaxy groups
summary: The impact of AGN feedback on the hot gas content of galaxy groups remains a key uncertainty in galaxy formation and its connection to the large scale structure of the Universe. We aim to compare the XMM-Newton Group AGN Project (X-GAP) sample to the hydrodynamical FLAMINGO simulations, which span a wide range of AGN feedback prescriptions. We construct X-GAP analogues by forward-modelling the full selection function, including detection and observational systematics, and generate end-to-end XMM-Newton mock observations analysed consistently with the data. We study multiple observables, including the L--T and Mgas--T relations, number of groups, mean temperature, and velocity dispersion, accounting for their covariance. The forward model accurately recovers input luminosities, gas masses, and core-excised temperatures for regular systems, enabling direct comparison in observable space. The normalisation of the scaling relations is the best discriminator between feedback models, while cosmic variance introduces > 20% fluctuations in the number of detected systems, making counts alone a weak discriminator. Models with intermediate feedback strength provide the best agreement with X-GAP, with the fgas-2sigma model yielding the lowest tension of only 0.8sigma, while the most extreme feedback scenario (fgas-8sigma) is ruled out at > 4sigma. Our results indicate that the thermodynamic properties of galaxy groups favour feedback stronger than the fiducial FLAMINGO calibration, but disfavour the most ejective models. This highlights the importance of combining forward modelling and multi-observable constraints to probe the fate of hot baryons in low-mass haloes.

AI.tldr: This study uses forward modelling to compare X-ray observations of galaxy groups with simulations, finding that moderate AGN feedback best explains the hot gas properties, while extreme feedback models are inconsistent with the data.
AI.motivation: To understand the impact of AGN feedback on the hot gas content of galaxy groups, which is crucial for galaxy formation and its link to large scale structure in the Universe.
AI.method: Comparison of XMM-Newton Group AGN Project (X-GAP) sample to hydrodynamical FLAMINGO simulations covering diverse AGN feedback models; construction of X-GAP analogues via forward-modelling selection functions, mock observations, and consistent data analysis; study of scaling relations and group properties accounting for covariance.
AI.result: Forward modelling recovers key observables accurately; normalization of scaling relations effectively differentiates feedback models; cosmic variance limits the utility of group number counts alone; intermediate feedback models best match observations; strongest feedback models are statistically ruled out.
AI.conclusion: Galaxy group thermodynamic properties prefer AGN feedback stronger than fiducial FLAMINGO calibration but exclude extreme ejective feedback scenarios, emphasizing the need for multi-observable forward modelling to constrain baryon fate in low-mass haloes.

title: Rotation Measure Substructures Induced by the Ponderomotive Force of Inertial \alfven Waves
summary: The rotation measure (RM) and dispersion measure (DM) of fast radio bursts (FRBs) serve as critical probes of the magneto-ionic environments along the line of sight. The significant temporal evolution of RM observed in some repeating FRBs is generally attributed to the local environment of the source, since the intergalactic medium is not expected to vary on such short timescales. Recent observations of repeating FRB 20201124A and FRB 20220529 exhibit complex RM phenomenology, including large-amplitude global fluctuations and short-term substructures. Here, we attribute these short-term RM variations to the ponderomotive force exerted by inertial \alfven~waves (IAWs). We propose that IAWs, generated via magnetic reconnection or turbulent cascades in a low-$β$ plasma, induce nonlinear density perturbations in the source environment. We demonstrate that the resulting plasma density redistribution can produce RM suppression consistent with observed substructures. This model presents a physically motivated mechanism for the short-term RM variability observed in active repeaters. It demonstrates that such fluctuations can arise from wave-driven density cavitation within a broad, coupled parameter space involving wave amplitude, plasma density, and temperature, thereby characterizing the localized plasma dynamics required to produce the observed RM jitters.

AI.tldr: Short-term RM fluctuations in repeating FRBs arise from plasma density changes driven by inertial Alfvén waves, offering a new explanation for observed RM variability.
AI.motivation: The motivation is to understand the origin of significant short-term RM variations in repeating FRBs, which cannot be explained by the stable intergalactic medium, by identifying a local, physically plausible mechanism involving wave-plasma interactions.
AI.method: The authors model the generation of inertial Alfvén waves via magnetic reconnection or turbulence in low-beta plasma, analyze how the ponderomotive force causes nonlinear density perturbations, and demonstrate that these density changes suppress RM to match observational substructures.
AI.result: This paper presents a model explaining short-term rotation measure (RM) variations observed in repeating fast radio bursts (FRBs) using the ponderomotive force of inertial Alfvén waves (IAWs) in a low-beta plasma environment. It attributes RM substructures to wave-driven plasma density perturbations caused by magnetic reconnection or turbulent cascades, providing a physically motivated explanation for RM variability in active repeaters.
AI.conclusion: The study concludes that nonlinear plasma density perturbations induced by IAWs can account for the complex RM variability seen in repeating FRBs, linking observed RM substructures to localized plasma dynamics in the source environment.

title: Intergalactic Magnetic Field constraints from detected very high-energy Gamma-Ray Bursts using the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory
summary: Defined as the magnetic field permeating cosmic voids, the Intergalactic Magnetic Field (IGMF) is thought to be a relic of the Big Bang, tracing a primordial magnetic seed at the origin of all astrophysical fields. Yet, it has thus far escaped detection. Lower limits on the IGMF strength can be established by observing very high-energy (VHE) photons from extragalactic sources. Specifically, this can be achieved by characterising the time-delayed secondary emission induced by highly energetic transient sources, such as gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). Most studies exclude values of the IGMF below $10^{-17}\;\mathrm{G}$ by comparing the expected effect to the sensitivity curves of various instruments in the $\mathrm{GeV}$ range or above. In this work, we simulate CTAO observation data under realistic observation conditions and perform spectral-temporal fits to estimate the constraints CTAO will bring on the IGMF once fully deployed. We apply the methodology to simulated sources with properties comparable to the few GRBs detected at VHE. In particular, we show that CTAO will probe strengths up to $\sim 10^{-15}\;\mathrm{G}$ when detecting sources similar to GRBs 221009A and 190114C. We also show that existing observations of GRB 221009A by the first CTAO Large Sized Telescope LST-1 favour a strength of $3\times 10^{-17}\;\mathrm{G}$.

AI.tldr: Simulations show the upcoming CTAO observatory can significantly improve lower limits on the IGMF strength by analyzing very high-energy gamma-ray bursts, probing fields up to ~10^{-15} G.
AI.motivation: To detect or better constrain the elusive Intergalactic Magnetic Field believed to be a relic of the Big Bang by leveraging the improved capabilities of next-generation VHE observatories like CTAO to observe delayed secondary gamma-ray emission from energetic transient extragalactic sources.
AI.method: The study uses spectral-temporal fitting on realistic simulated observation data from CTAO targeting VHE transient sources (GRBs), comparing expected secondary emission delays to instrument sensitivity, alongside analysis of early real observations from the LST-1 telescope.
AI.result: The paper investigates constraints on the Intergalactic Magnetic Field (IGMF) strength through simulations of very high-energy gamma-ray observations from transient sources like gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), using data expected from the forthcoming CTAO observatory. By performing spectral-temporal fits on simulated CTAO data for GRBs resembling past VHE detections, it demonstrates that CTAO can constrain IGMF strengths up to ~10^{-15} G. Additionally, it uses initial CTAO LST-1 observations of GRB 221009A to suggest a current lower limit around 3×10^{-17} G.
AI.conclusion: CTAO observations, both simulated and preliminary real data, are capable of setting stronger lower bounds on the IGMF, potentially detecting fields stronger than previously constrained (~10^{-17} G), advancing our understanding of primordial cosmic magnetism.

title: Variance-aware model discrimination with the Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect of the 21 cm background (SZE-21cm)
summary: The sky-averaged redshifted 21 cm signal from Cosmic Dawn is a uniquely sensitive tracer of early heating and ionisation, but it remains challenging to measure directly. The Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect of the 21 cm background (SZE-21cm) provides a complementary route: Comptonisation of the incident low-frequency background by hot electrons in galaxy clusters produces a spectral distortion that can be recovered as a difference between the line of sight through a galaxy cluster and a nearby blank-sky reference, and is therefore naturally compatible with interferometric observations. We use semi-numerical simulations of the global 21 cm background, together with a relativistic scattering kernel built from the Maxwell-Juttner electron distribution, to assess how well the SZE-21cm separates physically distinct Cosmic Dawn scenarios. The model suite varies star-formation efficiency, X-ray spectral hardness, heating timing, and the suppression of low-mass sources; SZE-21cm spectra are computed over 45-200 MHz. Separability is quantified through feature-based summaries, standardised residual spectra, and a band-integrated pairwise separability index that combines seed-to-seed scatter with an astrophysical variance layer derived from coeval ON-aperture / OFF-annulus statistics. The resulting indices are intrinsic and instrument-free, and therefore upper bounds on what a real experiment with finite thermal noise can achieve. Heating-timing variations produce the strongest separations, while the X-ray hardness variations explored here are nearly degenerate with the fiducial case once the ON-OFF variance is included. We also propagate an EDGES-like benchmark curve as a morphological stress test of the framework, not as a physically validated model, illustrating how anomalous global-signal morphologies would map into the SZE-21cm.

AI.tldr: This paper uses simulations to show that spectral distortions in the 21 cm background caused by hot electrons in galaxy clusters can differentiate Cosmic Dawn scenarios, especially based on heating timing, providing a viable indirect measurement method complementary to direct observations.
AI.motivation: Direct measurement of the sky-averaged redshifted 21 cm signal from Cosmic Dawn is difficult; the SZE-21cm effect offers a complementary approach by leveraging cluster electron Comptonisation to distinguish Cosmic Dawn scenarios via spectral distortions compatible with interferometric techniques.
AI.method: Semi-numerical simulations of the global 21 cm background integrated with a relativistic scattering kernel based on the Maxwell-Juttner electron distribution to model the SZE-21cm spectral distortions across 45-200 MHz.
AI.result: The study finds heating-timing variations yield the most significant separations in SZE-21cm spectra among scenarios, while variations in X-ray spectral hardness are largely degenerate with the fiducial model under observational variance; intrinsic separability indices provide upper limits for realistic experimental conditions; EDGES-like morphologies map consistently into the SZE-21cm framework demonstrating its diagnostic utility.
AI.conclusion: SZE-21cm spectral distortions serve as a robust, instrument-independent probe to separate astrophysical models of Cosmic Dawn, particularly sensitive to heating timing variations, with potential applicability to future interferometric observations despite challenges in X-ray hardness discrimination.

title: Substructure in redMaPPer clusters and its impact on X-ray morphology and scaling relations
summary: We statistically quantified the prevalence and properties of substructure in optical galaxy clusters and directly investigated its impact on X-ray morphology and scaling relations, leveraging new data from the DECaLS Legacy Survey and the SRG/eROSITA all-sky survey. We applied the hierarchical density-based clustering algorithm HDBSCAN to the redMaPPer galaxy cluster catalog to identify and characterize substructure from the probabilistic membership assignments. We then cross-matched this sample with the eROSITA X-ray morphology catalog to correlate optical substructure with a comprehensive set of X-ray morphological parameters. Finally, we analyzed the scaling relation between X-ray luminosity and optical richness for clusters with and without substructure. Substructure is a common feature, present in approximately 40% of clusters; a quarter of the full sample exhibits a fractional contribution to richness in excess of 35%. We find a highly significant correlation between optical substructure and disturbed X-ray morphologies, a trend that is strongest for high-mass clusters. The clusters with substructure also drive a stronger redshift evolution in the scatter of the Lx-lambda relation. At low redshifts (z<0.2), they display a systematically higher X-ray luminosity at fixed richness compared to relaxed systems. We attribute the enhanced effect of mergers on X-ray properties at low redshifts to the increased density contrast of low-redshift cool cores and longer substructure survival times, which are possibly due to the suppression of disruptive mixing by effects such as magnetic draping. At lower cluster richness, a discordance between X-ray morphology and the merging state indicates a growing relative importance of active galactic nucleus feedback in governing X-ray morphology.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies optical substructure in galaxy clusters and links it to disturbed X-ray morphology and scaling relation variations, revealing merger-driven effects modulated by redshift and feedback processes.
AI.motivation: To statistically quantify substructure prevalence and properties in optical galaxy clusters and directly investigate its impact on X-ray morphology and scaling relations using new, comprehensive survey data.
AI.method: We applied the hierarchical density-based clustering algorithm HDBSCAN to the redMaPPer galaxy cluster catalog for substructure identification, then cross-matched with eROSITA X-ray morphology data, and analyzed scaling relations between X-ray luminosity and optical richness.
AI.result: Substructure is present in ~40% of clusters; a significant correlation exists between optical substructure and disturbed X-ray morphologies, especially in high-mass clusters. Clusters with substructure show stronger redshift evolution in Lx-lambda scatter, with higher X-ray luminosity at fixed richness at low redshifts.
AI.conclusion: Mergers significantly affect X-ray properties at low redshifts due to enhanced cool core contrasts and substructure survival, while AGN feedback increasingly influences X-ray morphology in lower richness clusters where morphology and merging state diverge.

title: Multi-tracers, multi-surveys: data-driven EFT prior calibration from the PFS--DESI overlap
comment: 15+9 pages, most likely too many words; 6 tables, 9 figures; main results in Figure 2-3. Code is available at this repo: https://github.com/MinhMPA/PFSxDESI-multi-fish. It takes two
summary: Marginalizing over roughly 12 effective-field-theory (EFT) nuisance parameters per tracer per redshift bin is the dominant systematic cost in full-shape galaxy power spectrum analyses. Simulation-based priors (SBP) can tighten these parameters but rely on N-body simulations and halo-occupation-distribution (HOD) models. We propose multi-survey priors: a data-driven alternative that calibrates EFT parameters from the multi-tracer analysis of overlapping spectroscopic surveys. In the $\sim\!1{,}200\;\text{deg}^2$ Prime Focus Spectrograph (PFS)--Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) overlap at $0.6<z<1.6$, up to 4 tracers (PFS-ELG, DESI-ELG, DESI-LRG, DESI-QSO) and 10 cross-spectra per redshift bin provide model-independent constraints on the DESI nuisance parameters. Cross-spectra between different galaxy populations carry zero stochastic contribution, cleanly separating shot noise from signal. Exporting the calibrated priors to the full $14{,}000\;\text{deg}^2$ DESI footprint of the DESI LRG1--3, ELG1--2 and QSO samples improves $σ(fσ_8)$ by 8\% (7--25\% per sample) and $σ(M_ν)$ by 54\% (46--71\% per sample) at $k_{\rm max}=0.20\,h\,\mathrm{Mpc}^{-1}$. A parameter importance decomposition reveals that the dominant driver is the calibration of the $b_1σ_8$ prior -- constrained from a flat prior to $σ\approx 0.17$ by the multi-tracer Fisher -- which accounts for $\sim\!70\%$ of the $fσ_8$ gain and $\sim\!97\%$ of the $M_ν$ gain by breaking the $b_1σ_8$--$fσ_8$ degeneracy intrinsic to single-tracer analyses. Multi-survey prior calibration parallels the SBP approach, which tightens $b_1$ through HOD model assumptions; multi-survey priors provide a model-independent consistency check on these assumptions and generalize to arbitrary combinations of overlapping spectroscopic surveys.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces multi-survey priors, a data-driven method leveraging overlapping spectroscopic galaxy surveys to calibrate EFT nuisance parameters, improving cosmological parameter constraints without relying on simulation-based models.
AI.motivation: Marginalization over numerous EFT nuisance parameters per tracer and redshift bin significantly increases systematic uncertainties in galaxy power spectrum analyses, and current tightening methods depend on simulations and modeling assumptions that may introduce bias.
AI.method: The authors use a multi-tracer Fisher analysis of up to four tracers and their cross-spectra in overlapping spectroscopic survey regions to obtain model-independent constraints on nuisance parameters, particularly calibrating the $b_1σ_8$ prior, then export these calibrated priors to a larger survey footprint to enhance cosmological parameter inference.
AI.result: Applying multi-survey priors in the DESI survey improves uncertainties in $fσ_8$ by 8% and neutrino mass $M_ν$ by 54%, primarily through breaking degeneracies present in single-tracer analyses, thus providing tighter and model-independent calibrations that generalize across survey combinations.
AI.conclusion: Multi-survey priors offer a robust, model-independent alternative to simulation-based priors by exploiting overlapping survey data, significantly improving cosmological parameter constraints and providing a consistency check for HOD-based assumptions used in traditional approaches.

title: Fast radio burst dispersion is an unbiased tracer of matter on large scales
summary: The dispersion of fast radio bursts (FRBs) measures the column density of free electrons, tracing the diffuse ionized gas that contains more than $90\%$ of all baryons. On linear scales the FRB dispersion field is an approximately unbiased tracer of the matter distribution, an idea long assumed in the FRB large-scale structure literature and recently formalized by Zhou and Zhang [arXiv:2510.11022]. This follows from baryon-mass conservation, which forces the total baryon field to have unit linear bias, with dispersion inheriting this bias up to small corrections from the stellar and neutral-gas components. We show these corrections can be bounded at the percent level using existing galaxy and 21 cm surveys, and confirm with the FLAMINGO hydrodynamical simulations that the electron bias varies at the percent level across a wide range of feedback prescriptions. The dispersion-galaxy cross-power spectrum at linear scales directly constrains $B_8 \equiv σ_8(Ω_b/0.05)^{1/2}$, a baryonic analog of $S_8$, independently of feedback physics. Because most of the per-object variance in dispersion is cosmological signal rather than noise, $\sim\!10^5$ localized FRBs can match the statistical power of $\sim\!10^8$ weak-lensing galaxy shape measurements. FRB dispersion thus joins weak lensing and redshift-space distortions as a new unbiased tracer of matter on large scales.

AI.tldr: Fast radio burst dispersion measures ionized gas tracing baryons, acting as an unbiased matter tracer on large scales, confirmed by simulations and bounded corrections.
AI.motivation: To validate the assumption that FRB dispersion is an unbiased tracer of matter distribution and explore its potential for cosmological parameter constraints.
AI.method: The study combines theoretical bias arguments, observational data from galaxy and 21 cm surveys, and hydrodynamical simulations (FLAMINGO) to quantify and bound corrections to electron bias.
AI.result: Corrections to the electron bias are minimal (percent level), FRB dispersion-galaxy cross-power spectrum constrains a baryonic analog of $S_8$, and localized FRBs provide competitive cosmological measurement precision with fewer objects than weak lensing.
AI.conclusion: FRB dispersion is an unbiased large-scale tracer of matter and can precisely constrain cosmological parameters independently of feedback physics, comparable to weak lensing.

title: Recovering cosmological parameters from the mock gravitational wave data of the Einstein Telescope
summary: Einstein Telescope (ET) is a third-generation gravitational wave (GW) detector with tenfold better sensitivity compared to the advanced LIGO detectors. It will be capable of observing copious stellar mass binary black hole mergers upto a redshift of 10 which will make it especially useful for cosmography. We generate a mock gravitational wave event catalog for the Einstein Telescope and show the recoverability of either the Hubble constant ($H_0$) or the matter density parameter ($Ω_{\rm m}$). We present a simple, effective and fast technique for inferring $H_0$ (or $Ω_{\rm m}$) using the intrinsic chirp mass spectrum of black hole binaries, and investigate the efficacy of the method assuming the standard model of cosmology. If only $H_0$ has to be constrained, we find that at least one year of ET's observation will be required to achieve 1% uncertainty. With the same amount of observation, $Ω_{\rm m}$ can be constrained to within 4\% uncertainty. With ET operating as a standalone instrument, we show that the GW spectral sirens detected by it can constrain the Hubble constant.

AI.tldr: The paper discusses using the Einstein Telescope (ET) to constrain cosmological parameters like the Hubble constant and matter density via gravitational wave observations.
AI.motivation: ET's enhanced sensitivity allows detection of high redshift binary black hole mergers, providing a unique opportunity for cosmography through gravitational wave spectral sirens.
AI.method: They generate a mock catalog of gravitational wave events from binary black hole mergers detectable by ET and use an intrinsic chirp mass spectrum-based technique for parameter inference under the standard cosmological model.
AI.result: Using one year of ET data, the method can constrain $H_0$ within 1% and $Ω_{rm m}$ within 4% uncertainty, showing the efficacy of spectral siren analysis for cosmological measurements.
AI.conclusion: With one year of ET observations, the Hubble constant can be constrained to 1% uncertainty and the matter density parameter to 4%, demonstrating ET's capability as a standalone cosmological probe.

title: Generalizing the CPL Parametrization through Dark Sector Interaction
summary: We investigate a hierarchy of interacting dark energy (IDE) models featuring a non-gravitational coupling between dark matter and dark energy. Specifically, we examine scenarios where the background interaction kernel, $Q = 3H(δ+ ηa)ρ_\mathrm{de}$, allows for both constant and dynamical coupling parameters. Adopting the CPL parametrization for the dark energy equation of state, $w_\mathrm{de} = w_0 + w_a(1-a)$, we derive closed analytical expressions for the energy densities of dark matter and dark energy. Afterwards, we obtain observational constraints using joint combinations of DESI DR2 baryon acoustic oscillations, Pantheon$+$ Type Ia supernovae, and Planck$+$ACT compressed cosmic microwave background likelihoods. For constant coupling models, we find parametric deviations from $Λ$ ranging from $2.7σ$ to $2.9σ$; however, for interactions with dynamical couplings, these significances are reduced to $1.3σ$--$1.5σ$. Ultimately, our Bayesian model comparison reveals that no investigated IDE scenario is statistically preferred over the concordance $Λ$CDM model. These results highlight the necessity of reporting Bayesian evidence alongside conventional frequentist maximum-likelihood analyses to ensure robust cosmological claims concerning dark energy evolution and interaction.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes interacting dark energy models with constant and dynamic couplings using cosmological observations, finding no statistical preference over the standard ΛCDM model; it emphasizes the importance of Bayesian evidence in cosmological model selection.
AI.motivation: To investigate interacting dark energy models with both constant and dynamical non-gravitational couplings and to constrain them using the latest cosmological datasets in order to test their viability against the concordance ΛCDM cosmological model.
AI.method: Investigate IDE models with an interaction kernel Q=3H(δ+ηa)ρ_de, incorporating both constant and dynamic coupling parameters. Use the CPL parametrization for dark energy's equation of state to derive analytical expressions for energy densities. Perform observational constraints using DESI DR2 BAO, Pantheon+ SNIa, and Planck+ACT CMB data. Conduct Bayesian model comparison against ΛCDM.
AI.result: For constant coupling models, deviations from the ΛCDM model are observed at roughly 2.7σ to 2.9σ significance, while models with dynamical couplings show reduced significances around 1.3σ to 1.5σ. Bayesian evidence indicates that none of the IDE models outperform the standard ΛCDM cosmology statistically.
AI.conclusion: Despite some marginal deviations in constant coupling IDE models, no interacting dark energy scenario studied is statistically favored over the ΛCDM model, underscoring the necessity of Bayesian evidence reporting alongside frequentist analyses for robust cosmological conclusions.

title: On the Relation Between Field-Level Posteriors, Correlators, and their Likelihoods
summary: We develop a field-level posterior for cosmological data by marginalizing over initial conditions and noise in a general forward model. While our focus is on large-scale structure data, the results generalize to any weakly non-Gaussian observable. Moreover, the construction is non-perturbative with respect to the forward model and applies equally well to perturbative calculations, simulation-based predictions, and more general effective descriptions. Expanding the FLP around its Gaussian limit, we derive a general expression for the Fisher matrix and reorganize the field-level information into contributions associated with the connected correlators of the evolved field. This makes explicit which terms are captured by likelihood analyses based on the power spectrum, the bispectrum, or finite sets of summary statistics, and which are lost under compression. We recover the standard Gaussian-covariance result for the power spectrum, show that the Gaussian bispectrum likelihood reproduces the corresponding field-level contribution, and show how cross-covariances among summaries progressively reconstruct more of the full field-level information. As an application to the BAO scale, we show how the field contains all the information required for its optimal reconstruction in the presence of noise, and identify the contributions in the FLP needed to attain this limit. We also show that the reconstruction of the initial field arises naturally as a byproduct of our approach, yielding the optimal estimate of the initial conditions given the data and the noise. Our results provide a unified framework to compare field-level and correlator-based inference, to quantify the information loss induced by compression, and to explore the role of stochasticity.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a unified, non-perturbative field-level posterior framework for cosmological data that recovers existing correlator-based results, clarifies information capture and loss in data compression, and optimally reconstructs initial conditions and the BAO scale under noise.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive, non-perturbative framework for cosmological data analysis that captures all field-level information, clarifies the limitations of summary statistics-based methods, and achieves optimal parameter and initial condition inference despite observational noise.
AI.method: The authors construct a field-level posterior by marginalizing over initial conditions and noise using a general forward model, expand around the Gaussian limit to derive a Fisher matrix deconstruction into connected correlators, and apply the approach to BAO scale reconstruction and initial condition estimation.
AI.result: The paper develops a field-level posterior (FLP) framework for cosmological data analysis by marginalizing over initial conditions and noise, applicable broadly to weakly non-Gaussian observables beyond large-scale structure data. The approach is non-perturbative concerning the forward model and supports perturbative, simulation-based, and effective descriptions. By expanding the FLP around a Gaussian limit, the authors derive a general Fisher matrix expression, decomposing information into contributions from connected correlators of the evolved field. This decomposition explicitly delineates information captured or lost in analyses using power spectra, bispectra, or summary statistics, recovering known Gaussian-covariance results and illustrating progressive reconstruction of information via cross-covariances among summaries. The method is applied to baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) scale reconstruction, demonstrating optimal information extraction despite noise and naturally yielding an optimal initial condition estimate. The framework unifies field-level and correlator-based inference, quantifies compression-induced information loss, and clarifies stochasticity's role.
AI.conclusion: This framework unifies field-level and correlator-based cosmological inference, allowing precise quantification of information retention and loss in summary statistics, and enables optimal reconstruction of initial conditions and key scales like BAO even in noisy data contexts.

title: Microlensing of fast and slow compact objects
summary: Gravitational microlensing constraints on non-standard compact objects are conventionally derived assuming lenses trace the dark matter halo with velocities following a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. However, a variety of theoretical scenarios predict populations of compact objects whose velocities deviate dramatically from those of virialized halo dark matter -- ultrarelativistic primordial black holes from cosmic string collapse, mirror neutron stars, gravitationally kicked black hole merger remnants, dark matter nuggets, free floaters ejected from gravitationally bound systems, disk-formed compact objects, and so on. For a given Einstein crossing time, the speed-mass degeneracy inherent in it means that fast (slow) lenses produce events at larger (smaller) masses than spanned by standard windows, opening qualitatively new regions of parameter space. After deriving model-independent upper limits on the microlensing event rate, we obtain mass-dependent constraints on the density of lens populations with speeds spanning $10^{-4}c-10^{-1}c$ from surveys of M31 by Subaru-HSC and the LMC by OGLE with different observing cadences. We do this for two benchmark velocity distributions -- Maxwell-Boltzmann and Dirac delta -- and two spatial distributions -- uniform and NFW, and exclude lens densities and masses that differ from dark matter constraints by orders of magnitude. We examine the effect of the transverse motion of the source and observer relative to the lensing tube, which becomes significant for our slow lenses. We also show that, unlike in dark matter searches, for our fast lenses an increase in the cadence of observations would probe smaller masses without suppression of event rates from the finite source and wave optics effects.

AI.tldr: This paper generalizes gravitational microlensing constraints to encompass compact object populations with non-standard velocities, deriving robust limits and highlighting new parameter spaces informed by varying velocity and spatial distributions.
AI.motivation: Standard gravitational microlensing analyses assume lenses with velocities following a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution tracing the dark matter halo. However, various theoretical models predict compact objects with significantly different velocity distributions, motivating the need to explore how these deviations affect microlensing constraints and to open new parameter space regions.
AI.method: The paper derives model-independent upper limits on microlensing event rates and obtains mass-dependent constraints on lens population densities by analyzing microlensing data from Subaru-HSC and OGLE surveys. It considers two benchmark velocity distributions (Maxwell-Boltzmann and Dirac delta) and two spatial distributions (uniform and NFW) for compact objects with speeds from 10^{-4}c to 10^{-1}c.
AI.result: The study excludes lens densities and masses that deviate from typical dark matter constraints by orders of magnitude, identifies how fast and slow lens velocities shift the expected mass ranges for lensing events, and finds that increased observation cadence can probe smaller masses for fast lenses without event rate suppression. It also highlights the importance of transverse motions for slow lenses.
AI.conclusion: By incorporating non-standard velocity distributions and spatial profiles of compact objects, the paper provides expanded and more general microlensing constraints that reveal new allowable mass and density ranges, with significant implications for future survey strategies and theoretical model testing.

title: Testing template-fitting models for the multipoles of the two-point clustering of galaxy clusters
summary: The \textit{Euclid} satellite will deliver a catalogue of optically-selected galaxy clusters spanning from around $2000$ deg$^2$ in Data Release (DR) 1 to around $14\,000$ deg$^2$ in DR3. We assess the validity of cluster clustering (CC) models for template-fitting, which complements the full-shape methodology in providing cosmological information from the anisotropy of the redshift-space two-point correlation function (2PCF). Both will be used to analyse the cluster 2PCF multipoles in \textit{Euclid}. We analyse the multipoles of the two-point redshift-space clustering of galaxy clusters simulated with the semi-analytic \code{PINOCCHIO} code using third-order Lagrangian perturbation theory, assuming a \textit{Euclid} DR1-like footprint of 500 deg$^2$ in the Northern Hemisphere and 1400 deg$^2$ in the Southern Hemisphere. We estimate the first three even multipoles of the 2PCF and associated covariance matrix from 1000 DR1-like synthetic catalogues. We study the impact of the modelling of nonlinearities, halo bias, and photometric redshift uncertainties on the 2PCF. We apply three clustering models to the mock catalogues at $0<z<2$ and virial mass $M_{\rm vir}>10^{14}\;h^{-1}\,M_\odot$ under realistic and optimistic photometric redshift uncertainty scenarios. We formulate a set of permissive and conservative criteria that should be fulfilled by the multipole cut-off scales and validate against 100 mock catalogues via inference of the growth rate times the matter power spectrum normalisation parameter, $fσ_8$. We test the dispersion, Scoccimarro, and Taruya--Nishimichi--Saito models. We find that the simplest of the three -- the dispersion model -- yields unbiased inferences on $fσ_8$ from CC down to $10$ $h^{-1}$ Mpc in a DR1-like setting. All clustering models provide very similar goodness-of-fit metrics in the presence of DR1-like cluster redshift uncertainties.

AI.tldr: Evaluation of cluster clustering models using simulated Euclid DR1-like data shows that the simplest dispersion model reliably recovers cosmological growth rates despite photometric redshift uncertainties.
AI.motivation: To validate cluster clustering (CC) models for template-fitting that complement the full-shape methodology, facilitating robust cosmological parameter inference from Euclid satellite cluster data, particularly in light of photometric redshift uncertainties and nonlinear effects.
AI.method: Analysis of the redshift-space two-point correlation function (2PCF) multipoles of galaxy clusters using three clustering models (dispersion, Scoccimarro, and Taruya--Nishimichi--Saito) applied to simulated synthetic catalogues generated with the semi-analytic PINOCCHIO code and third-order Lagrangian perturbation theory.
AI.result: The dispersion model provides unbiased estimates of the growth rate parameter $fσ_8$ down to 10 $h^{-1}$ Mpc for a DR1-like footprint and photometric uncertainties, with all three tested models showing similar goodness-of-fit metrics under realistic conditions.
AI.conclusion: Cluster clustering models, especially the dispersion model, are validated for use in Euclid data analysis to extract cosmological information from cluster 2PCF multipoles, supporting the methodology for growth rate measurements with realistic photometric redshift errors.

title: Geometric Constraints on the Pre-Recombination Expansion History from the Hubble Tension
summary: I perform a model-independent reconstruction of the background pre-recombination expansion history of the Universe. I find that purely early-time resolutions to the Hubble tension, satisfying the geometric CMB constraints, exist at the background level. This class of solutions requires a smooth transition around matter-radiation equality, characterized by a $\simeq 15\%$ expansion rate enhancement prior to recombination. This result serves as a blueprint for future model-building approaches, providing a background stress-test for Hubble tension proposals.

AI.tldr: The study finds early-time expansions that resolve the Hubble tension by boosting the Universe's expansion rate by ~15% before recombination while matching CMB constraints.
AI.motivation: To explore purely early-time modifications to the expansion history as a geometric and background-level resolution to the Hubble tension, guiding future cosmological models.
AI.method: A model-independent reconstruction approach of the pre-recombination expansion history is utilized, focusing on background cosmology constraints from the Cosmic Microwave Background.
AI.result: The paper achieves a model-independent reconstruction of the Universe's pre-recombination expansion history, identifying early-time solutions to the Hubble tension compatible with CMB geometric constraints. These solutions feature a smooth transition near matter-radiation equality with approximately a 15% increase in expansion rate before recombination. This provides a foundational framework for future cosmological model developments addressing the Hubble tension.
AI.conclusion: Early-time modifications to the expansion history featuring a smooth transition near matter-radiation equality can resolve the Hubble tension at the background level without violating CMB geometry constraints.
